# The Case for Funding Curiosity

## Why a Society Should Pay for Research Without Knowing What It Will Find

### Introduction

Every year, governments allocate public money to research whose practical payoff is uncertain, distant, or entirely unknown at the moment of funding. A mathematician studies the distribution of prime numbers. A physicist measures the spin states of trapped ions. A botanist catalogues the chemistry of an obscure fungus. None of these projects promises a product, a cure, or a return within the budgeting horizon of any minister. And yet the argument of this essay is that a society which stops paying for such work, and funds only research with a clear and near-term application, makes itself poorer in a way it will struggle to perceive until it is too late.

This is not a comfortable argument to make in a tight fiscal climate. When hospitals are stretched and schools need roofs, the claim that we should spend on the mating habits of beetles or the topology of abstract surfaces can sound like the special pleading of a privileged class. I want to take that objection seriously rather than wave it away. The case for curiosity-driven research is strong, but it is not unconditional, and the honest version of it admits real costs and real failures. What follows is an attempt at the honest version.

### What we mean by curiosity-driven research

By curiosity-driven, or basic, research I mean inquiry whose primary aim is understanding rather than application. The distinction is not perfectly sharp. Plenty of applied work generates deep understanding, and plenty of basic work is done with a half-formed eye on eventual use. The cleaner way to draw the line is by the criterion used to decide what to fund. Applied research is justified by a problem it is meant to solve. Basic research is justified by a question it is meant to answer, with no commitment that the answer will be useful.

This matters because the two kinds of work fail differently and pay off differently. Applied research that fails to solve its problem has failed on its own terms. Basic research that fails to find a use has not necessarily failed at all, because use was never the standard. The standard was whether we now understand something we did not before. A society that funds only the first kind has quietly decided that understanding has no value unless it can be cashed in, and that is a decision worth examining rather than assuming.

### The argument from serendipity

The most frequently cited case for basic research is that the most valuable applications often come from work that was not aiming at them. The examples are familiar. The mathematics of number theory, pursued for centuries as the purest of pure inquiry, now secures every online transaction through public-key cryptography. The study of bacterial immune systems, an esoteric corner of microbiology, produced CRISPR gene editing. Investigations into the strange behaviour of light and matter at small scales gave us the laser, which was for years a solution in search of a problem and is now in every checkout scanner and fibre-optic cable.

The serendipity argument is genuinely strong, but it is also frequently overstated, and the overstatement is worth flagging because it weakens the case when critics notice it. The fact that some basic research led to enormous applications does not show that basic research is a reliable route to applications. It may be that the famous cases are famous precisely because they are rare, and that for every number theory there are a thousand lines of inquiry that led nowhere of practical consequence. The serendipity argument, taken alone, suffers from survivorship bias. We remember the lottery winners and forget the tickets.

So the argument has to be made more carefully. The defensible version is not that basic research reliably produces applications, but that applications of the largest kind, the ones that reshape whole industries, disproportionately trace back to work that could not have been justified by its eventual use, because that use was unimaginable at the time. If that is true, and the historical record gives reasonable support to it, then a funding system that demands a foreseeable application as a condition of funding will systematically miss exactly the largest payoffs. It will fund the foreseeable and starve the transformative. The serendipity argument, properly stated, is not about averages. It is about the shape of the tail.

### The argument from time horizons

Closely related is the problem of time. The lag between a basic discovery and its application is often measured in decades. The geometry that Riemann developed in the 1850s sat unused by physics until Einstein needed it for general relativity sixty years later. The work on the quantum behaviour of semiconductors that underpins the modern computer drew on physics from the early twentieth century. These horizons are far longer than any electoral cycle, any venture-capital fund's lifetime, and most corporate planning windows.

This creates a straightforward market failure of the textbook kind. A private firm cannot capture the returns on an investment that will pay off in forty years, possibly to a competitor, possibly in an industry that does not yet exist. The returns are real but they are diffuse, delayed, and uncapturable by the investor. Under those conditions, private actors will rationally underinvest, not because they are short-sighted but because they are responding correctly to the incentives they face. This is the classic justification for public provision of a public good, and basic knowledge fits the definition unusually well. Once discovered, a piece of knowledge can be used by everyone at once without being used up, which is the textbook property of non-rivalry, and it is very hard to exclude others from using it, which is non-excludability. Goods with both properties are chronically undersupplied by markets, and the standard remedy is public funding.

The time-horizon argument is, to my mind, the strongest part of the case, because it does not depend on cherry-picked success stories. It is a structural claim about incentives that holds regardless of how often basic research succeeds. Even a sceptic who doubts the serendipity stories should accept that if long-horizon knowledge has value, the private sector will underprovide it, and someone with a longer horizon must step in. The natural candidate is the public, acting through the state, because the public is the entity whose horizon is, in principle, indefinite.

### The argument from public good and shared inheritance

There is a third argument that is less often made and is, I think, underrated. Knowledge is part of the inheritance a society passes to its successors. We did not invent the calculus, or the structure of DNA, or the periodic table; we received them, and we will pass on whatever we add. A generation that consumed the scientific inheritance of its predecessors while adding nothing, because it judged that addition insufficiently profitable, would be living off capital it did not replenish. There is something both unjust and imprudent in that posture, in the way that there is something wrong with a generation that lets the cathedrals it inherited fall down because it would rather not pay the maintenance.

This argument is more value-laden than the others, and a hard-headed reader may find it soft. I include it not because it can carry the case alone but because the case is not purely economic. Part of why a society funds astronomy and palaeontology and the study of dead languages is that it takes understanding the universe and its own past to be among the things a civilisation is for. That is a claim about values, not about returns, and it should be made openly rather than disguised as economics. When defenders of basic science pretend that every grant is secretly an investment with a positive expected monetary return, they concede the very ground they should be contesting, which is that money is the only measure that counts.

### The strongest counterarguments

Now to the other side, which deserves better than the caricature it usually receives.

The first serious objection is opportunity cost. Public money is finite, and a pound spent on the topology of four-dimensional manifolds is a pound not spent on a vaccine trial, a flood defence, or a clinical study that would save identifiable lives within the year. The serendipity argument says the manifold work might pay off enormously in forty years, but might is doing heavy lifting, and the vaccine trial pays off in twelve months with high probability. A decision-maker who must choose is not being philistine when she prefers the certain near-term good to the speculative long-term one. She is making a defensible judgement about risk and time that the basic-research advocate too often dismisses.

The second objection is accountability. Public money should be spent in ways the public can scrutinise and to some degree direct. Curiosity-driven research, almost by definition, resists this. The researcher cannot say in advance what she will find, which means she cannot be held to a deliverable, which means the public is asked to write a cheque on trust. In a democracy this is genuinely uncomfortable. It concentrates the power to decide what is worth knowing in the hands of expert committees that are not elected and whose judgements about which questions matter may reflect the fashions and blind spots of their fields. The peer-review system that allocates basic-research funding is known to be conservative, to favour the established, and to struggle with genuinely novel proposals, which undercuts the very transformative payoff the serendipity argument relies on.

The third objection is that the dichotomy may be false. Much of the most fertile research, the critic can argue, lives in what has been called Pasteur's quadrant: work that is both fundamental and use-inspired, that seeks deep understanding precisely because it is grappling with a practical problem. Pasteur did foundational microbiology while trying to stop wine from spoiling and sheep from dying. If the richest vein is use-inspired basic research, then the pure, application-blind ideal defended in the first half of this essay may be funding the wrong thing, and a system that asks researchers to articulate a possible eventual use is not philistine but is simply steering money toward the most productive quadrant.

These are good arguments. I do not think they defeat the case, but a defender who does not feel their force is not paying attention.

### A reply that concedes what it should

The honest reply is not to deny the costs but to argue about proportion. The opportunity-cost objection is decisive against spending most of the science budget on curiosity-driven work, but almost nobody proposes that. In most countries basic research is a minority share of public research spending, and the question is whether that minority share should be cut to zero or near it, not whether it should crowd out vaccines. At realistic proportions, the marginal pound of basic research is not competing with the marginal vaccine; it is competing with marginal applied research whose expected long-run value may well be lower precisely because it is confined to the foreseeable.

On accountability, the right response is to improve the mechanisms rather than abandon the enterprise. The conservatism of peer review is a real defect, and there is a strong case for funding instruments that deliberately back high-risk, high-variance work, fund people rather than projects, and tolerate a high failure rate as the price of the occasional transformative success. The accountability objection is an argument for better institutions, not for defunding.

On Pasteur's quadrant, I simply concede the point and narrow my claim. The strongest version of my thesis is not that pure, use-blind research should dominate, but that a portfolio which contains no application-blind inquiry at all will systematically miss the discoveries that no one knew to look for. Use-inspired basic research is wonderful and should be funded generously. But use-inspired research is still steered by current conceptions of use, and the history of science is in large part the history of discoveries that overturned those conceptions. Some fraction of the budget should be reserved for inquiry accountable only to the standard of whether it is true and deep, precisely because that is the only kind that can find what we did not know to want.

### A note on what the argument does not claim

It is worth being explicit about the limits of the case, because overclaiming is how good arguments lose credibility. Nothing here shows that any particular field deserves funding, that current funding levels are too low rather than misallocated, or that the institutions we have are the right ones to disburse the money. A reader could accept every word of this essay and still believe that a given national science agency is bloated, captured, or spending on the wrong questions. The argument is about a category of inquiry and why it has a claim on the public purse, not a defence of any existing budget line or bureaucracy. Those are separate questions, and conflating them is a move that defenders of the status quo and its critics both make too easily. Keeping them apart is part of arguing in good faith.

### What follows for policy

If the argument holds, the policy implication is modest and specific. It is not that we should pour unlimited money into ivory towers. It is that a mature research system should hold a deliberate portfolio: a large applied component answerable to present needs, a substantial use-inspired component in Pasteur's quadrant, and a protected minority allocated to curiosity-driven work that is judged by the quality of the questions and the rigour of the inquiry rather than by any promised application. The protected minority should be funded through instruments that tolerate failure, back unconventional people, and resist the gravitational pull toward the safe and the foreseeable.

The size of that protected minority is a genuine question on which reasonable people differ, and I will not pretend to a precise figure. The argument of this essay establishes that it should be greater than zero and that the burden of proof lies on those who would shrink it, not that it should be any particular number. That is a more limited conclusion than the rhetoric of science advocacy usually reaches for, and it is more defensible for being limited.

### Conclusion

The case for funding curiosity rests on three legs of unequal strength. The serendipity argument is vivid but vulnerable to survivorship bias and should be stated as a claim about the shape of the payoff distribution rather than its average. The time-horizon argument is the sturdiest, a clean instance of market failure that holds regardless of how often basic research succeeds. The public-good and inheritance argument is the most value-laden and should be made openly as a claim about what a civilisation is for rather than smuggled in as economics.

Against these stand real objections about opportunity cost, accountability, and the possibility that use-inspired work is the more fertile ground. The right response to these objections is not denial but proportion and institutional reform. A society should not spend most of its research money on curiosity. But a society that spends none of it has decided that it will only ever find what it already knew to look for, and that is a quiet but profound impoverishment of its own future. The wager of basic research is that the universe is stranger and more useful than our current sense of use can imagine. The historical record suggests it is a wager worth keeping a place at the table for, even, and especially, when the budget is tight.
